routes.title: Reductive algebraic groups, Part II: modular representations and generic GL3 lattices
routes.reason: Neither the Tau Ceti roadmaps (Reductive algebraic groups, Root systems) nor any proposed roadmap plans modular rational representations of reductive groups, Frobenius kernels and their injective envelopes, affine Weyl group and alcove combinatorics with the p-dot action, Deligne–Lusztig representations and the reduction of their lattices, or the Loewy-structure theory of §4.1.1. These are the general direction of Tau Ceti's Reductive algebraic groups roadmap, extended to modular representations; the GL3 lattice theorem 4.1.9 is its target.
routes.brief:
Reductive algebraic groups, Part II: modular representations and generic GL3 lattices, for Le–Le Hung–Levin–Morra, "Serre weights and Breuil's lattice conjecture in dimension three" (Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020), e5; LLHLM20). It extends Tau Ceti's Reductive algebraic groups roadmap (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ReductiveGroups) and imports Root systems (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/RootSystems: Weyl groups as Coxeter systems, Bruhat order), Classical groups (highest weights of GL_n), Mathlib's Rep and Tau Ceti's module socle; characteristic-zero complete reducibility is not used in characteristic p.

Final theorems, as LLHLM20 states them. Theorem 4.1.9: let R be a 13-generic Deligne–Lusztig representation of G = ∏_{v∈S} GL3(k_v) over E and σ ∈ JH(R̄), with R^σ the lattice with irreducible cosocle σ. Then (1) d_gph(σ, κ) = d^σ_rad(κ) for all κ ∈ JH(R̄), and the Loewy length of R̄^σ is 3f − Def_R(σ) + 1 (f = Σ_v [k_v : F_p]); (2) the radical extension graph and (3) the full extension graph of R̄^σ are predicted by the extension graph: κ1 points to κ2 iff d_gph(κ1, κ2) = 1 and d_gph(σ, κ1) ≤ d_gph(σ, κ2); (4) R̄^σ is rigid; (5) if R^κ ↪ R^σ is saturated then p^{d_gph(κ,σ)} R^σ ↪ R^κ is saturated. Theorem 2.1.10: for 6-deep Serre weights F, F′ of G, Ext¹_G(F, F′) ≠ 0 iff F and F′ are adjacent. Theorem 4.2.7 on the Weyl module V_μ restricted to G (its constituents Tr_{V_μ}: Λ_{⪯(η′,0)} ≅ JH(V_μ|_G), its layers by graph distance, and a multiplicity-free submodule with predicted extension graph), and Theorem 4.2.16 (the lower-alcove, defect-zero base case).

Cover, in this order: (a) the combinatorics of §§1.4, 2.1 and 2.3 — the concrete root datum of GL3 and of the restriction of scalars, the affine and extended affine Weyl groups W_a, W̃, W̃^∨ with the p-dot action, p-alcoves and depth, W̃⁺, W̃₁⁺, the involution w̃ ↦ w̃*, the translation charts 𝔗𝔯_μ and their change of centre, p-regular Serre weights F(λ) and Herzig's classification, adjacency and the extension graph (with its interior degree 7·#J), the nine-point set Σ₀, obvious/inner and outer/shadow weights, defect, the admissible set Adm(η) with Tables 1–2 and Figure 2; (b) Deligne–Lusztig representations R_s(μ), their genericity and irreducibility, V(τ̄) and the map ℛ, and the Jordan–Hölder factors of their reductions (Propositions 2.3.5, 2.3.7, Corollaries 2.3.11, 2.3.13); (c) the general theory of §4.1.1 for a finite abelian category: radical, socle and Loewy filtrations, rigidity, multiplicity-free objects, closed subsets, extension graphs and paths, duality (Propositions 4.1.1–4.1.7); (d) the modular representation theory of §4.2: Frobenius kernels G1T, the injective envelopes Q̂1(μ) and Q1(μ) (Theorem 4.2.1), p-bounded and deep modules, the translation principle, the structure of Q1(μ) and of Weyl modules for GL3 with Tables 5–6, the Ext¹ computations (Lemma 4.2.6, Propositions 4.2.9–4.2.12, with Proposition 4.2.9 corrected to the Ext¹ pattern of Tables 5–6), and the embedding construction (Lemmas 4.2.13–4.2.14, Proposition 4.2.15), with the cited inputs of Jantzen's book, Pillen, Andersen, Andersen–Kaneda, Bowman–Doty–Martin, Alperin and Emerton–Gee–Savitt §4.1 stated and proved or explicitly imported; (e) the lattice theory of §4.3: saturated inclusions, saturation and cosocle distances, predicted strata, maximally saturated constituents and the defect induction (Propositions 4.3.14–4.3.19). Proposition 4.3.7 uses patched modules and local deformation rings: import them from GenericGL3SerreWeightsAndLattices (its pre-lattice stages only) and LocalGaloisDeformationRings L7, and never use Theorem 4.1.9 in the globalisation that proves it. Record the depth hypotheses exactly: as printed, Theorem 4.2.7(3) and Propositions 4.2.10, 4.2.12 and 4.2.15 assume μ 6-deep but apply Lemma 4.2.6 to constituents that are only 4-deep, so they need μ 8-deep (the extraction's sourceIssues); Proposition 4.2.9 holds only in the corrected form given by Tables 5–6. Coordinate with the concurrently proposed ReductiveGroupsIntegralRepresentationsPartII (Kisin–Pappas) for integral and modular representations of reductive groups and with the sibling extraction PAPER-LE-LEHUNG-LEVIN-ETAL-23, which reuses this roadmap id: one foundation for Deligne–Lusztig and Serre-weight combinatorics, not two.

routes.title: Algebraic modular forms, reduction and Serre weights, Part II: generic GL3 weights and Breuil lattices
routes.reason: AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights R15.4 is Serre's classical GL2 weight recipe and SerreWeightAndLevelOptimisation R20 is classical level and weight optimisation; no layer plans set-valued Serre weights for GL3 (Herzig's W^?), weak minimal patching functors, numerical and geometric Breuil–Mézard for GL3, cyclicity and gauges of patched lattices, or Breuil's lattice conjecture. This is the direction of AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights, so it is a Part II of it; the sibling extraction PAPER-LE-LEHUNG-LEVIN-ETAL-23 uses the same roadmap id. Area corrected from 'modular' to 'automorphic' by REV-PAPER-LE-LEHUNG-LEVIN-ETAL-20: 'modular' is the parent roadmap's atlas group, not a galaxy id in data/galaxies.json, and PAPER-LE-LEHUNG-LEVIN-ETAL-23, which proposes this same roadmap id, uses 'automorphic'.
routes.brief:
Algebraic modular forms, reduction and Serre weights, Part II: generic GL3 weights and Breuil lattices, for Le–Le Hung–Levin–Morra, "Serre weights and Breuil's lattice conjecture in dimension three" (Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020), e5; LLHLM20). It extends AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights, whose R15.4 is the classical GL2 weight recipe and does not own set-valued GL3 weights, minimal patching or lattice locality.

Final theorems, as LLHLM20 states them (global setup of §5.3: F/F⁺ CM with F/F⁺ unramified at all finite places, p unramified in F⁺ and every place of F⁺ above p split in F; G the definite unitary group; the Taylor–Wiles conditions and split ramification). Theorem 5.3.3 (weight part of Serre's conjecture): if r̄ : G_F → GL3(F) satisfies the Taylor–Wiles conditions, r̄|_{G_{F_ṽ}} is semisimple and 10-generic for all ṽ ∈ 𝒮, r̄ is automorphic and has split ramification, then W(r̄) = W^?(ρ̄_𝒮). Theorem 5.3.4 (mod p multiplicity one): for τ_𝒮 13-generic and σ ∈ W^?(ρ̄_𝒮, τ_𝒮) satisfying condition (5.1) of Theorem 5.1.1, S(U^p𝒢(𝒪_{F⁺,p}), (σ̄(τ_𝒮)^σ ∘ ∏ι_ṽ)^∨ ⊗ W_{Σ₀⁺})[𝔪] is one-dimensional over F. Theorem 5.3.1 (automorphy lifting for potentially crystalline r of Hodge–Tate weights (2,1,0) and tame type, with r̄ 10-generic and semisimple at p). Theorem 5.3.5 (Breuil's lattice conjecture): for r as in Theorem 5.3.1 and minimally ramified, and a 13-generic tame type, the lattice σ(τ)⁰ = σ(τ) ∩ S̃(U^p, W)[λ] depends only on {r|_{G_{F_ṽ}}}_{ṽ∈𝒮}. sourceIssues.printed: Let τ be a 3-generic type with lowest alcove presentation (s, µ) and let 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F′) be semisimple of shape w̃ = (w̃_j) ∈ W̃^∨. … Then W?(ρ̄, τ) … = {σ^{(s,µ+η)}_{(ω,a)} : (ω, a) ∈ Σ_{w̃^*}}

sourceIssues.reason: The proof invokes Corollary 2.3.11, which requires w̃^* ∈ W̲_a t_η. For other shapes the statement fails. Take f = 1, s = 1, μ 4-deep, and the semisimple Kisin module with A = v^{(1,0,0)} (height ≤ 1, shape t_{(1,0,0)}). Then ρ̄ = T^*_dd(𝔐̄) is 3-generic with ρ̄|_{I_K} ≅ τ̄(1, μ+(1,0,0)+η). The central character of W?(ρ̄) is that of F(μ+(1,0,0)), which differs from that of JH(σ̄(τ)) = JH(R̄_1(μ+η)) (F(μ+1̲)) by N(x)^2 ≠ 1, so W?(ρ̄,τ) = ∅. But Σ_{t_{ε_1}} = Σ_0 ∩ t_{ε_1}(r(Σ_0)) = {(ε_2,1), (ε_1,0), (ε_1+ε_2,0), (ε_1,1)} ≠ ∅, so the right-hand side is nonempty. Defence: the paper only ever uses shapes in Adm^∨(η), Table 2 lists only Adm(η), and the surrounding text (§3.4 introduction, Prop. 3.4.4) makes the intended scope clear. Independent check: Quote checked on p. 35. The hypothesis allows any semisimple 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F′) of shape w̃ ∈ W̲̃^∨. The proof is 'follows from Corollary 2.3.11 and Proposition 3.4.1', but Corollary 2.3.11 requires w̃ ∈ W̲_a t_η. I rechecked the counterexample. Take f = 1, s = 1, μ deep, A = v^(1,0,0) = diag(v,1,1). This matrix is in Mat_3(F[[v]]) and upper triangular mod v, so by [LLHLM18, Prop. 2.13, Lemma 2.14] it defines 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F) for h ≥ 1, semisimple of shape t_(1,0,0), with w̃* = t_(1,0,0). By Prop. 3.4.1 and Def. 2.3.6, V(ρ̄|_{I_K}) = R_1(μ+η+(1,0,0)), which is 3-generic for μ deep. All Jordan–Hölder factors of R̄_w(λ) have the central character given by λ restricted to Z, and W?(ρ̄) = R(JH(V(ρ̄|_{I_K}))) with R shifting the central character by a fixed amount. Compare the admissible shape t_1̲ (Table 2, 'Id' row, 6 weights), where V = R_1(μ+η+(1,1,1)) and the intersection is nonempty, so the central characters match there. For t_(1,0,0) the central character of W?(ρ̄) differs from that case by x ↦ x², which is nontrivial because p > 3. Hence W?(ρ̄,τ) = ∅. But Σ_{t_(1,0,0)} = {(ε1,0), (ε1,1), (ε2,1), (ε1+ε2,0)} ≠ ∅ (recomputed; W̃ acts through W̃^der). The same failure occurs inside Adm(η)X⁰(T). For example, A = v²·Id has shape t_(2,2,2), and Σ_{t_(2,2,2)} = Σ_{Id} has 6 elements. But ρ̄|_{I_K} is the t_1̲ case twisted by a character that changes the central character by x³ ≠ 1, so the left side is again empty. The reader's weaker fix 'w̃* ∈ W̲_a t_η X⁰(T̲)' therefore does not suffice. The applications (Prop. 3.4.4, Lemma 3.5.4, proofs of Lemma 3.5.9 and Thm 3.5.3) all use shapes in Adm^∨(η). By Remark 3.4.3 these have w̃* ∈ Adm(η) ⊂ W̲_a t_η, so no result downstream is affected. Versions: identical in v3 and v4 (p. 27).

In the paper's defence, both facts are elementary, and the fixes above use only what the proof already establishes.

sourceIssues.reason: The lemma assumes only p ≥ 2(h−1), and for p ∈ {2h−2, 2h−1} (e.g. h = 3, p = 5) one has 2(h−1) > p−2. For h = 3, p = 5 and ω_κ = (3,0,0), ⟨ω_κ, α^∨⟩ ≤ 3 < 4 for all positive coroots but ⟨ω_κ+ρ, α₀^∨⟩ = 5 = p, so ω_κ is on the upper wall and not in the lower alcove. For h ≥ 4, even p ≥ 2h does not put ω_κ in the lowest alcove, since that needs ⟨ω_κ, α₀^∨⟩ ≤ p−h. In the paper's defence, the conclusion (no extensions with characters) is true under the stated hypotheses by the argument above, and the paper only applies the lemma to GL₃ with p ≥ 5 and large genericity. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 83 (page image). §4.2.1 works with a general G of Coxeter number h (p. 79), and Lemma 4.2.4 assumes only p ⩾ 2(h−1). Alcoves are open (p. 9: connected components of the complement of the hyperplanes), and C0 is 'the p-restricted lower alcove' (p. 11). p-bounded means ⟨κ,α^∨⟩ < 2(h−1)p (p. 81), so ⟨ω_κ,α^∨⟩ ⩽ 2h−3. For GL3 (h = 3) with p = 5, which is allowed by the lemma and by p > 3 (§1.4), 2(h−1) = 4 > p−2 = 3. Take κ = pω_κ with ω_κ = (3,0,0). It is p-bounded (⟨κ,α0^∨⟩ = 15 < 20), but ⟨ω_κ+η,α0^∨⟩ = 5 = p, so ω_κ lies on the wall H_{α0,1} and not in C0. For general h, lying in C0 needs ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ ⩽ p−h, i.e. p ⩾ 3h−3. The conclusion (4.8) is still true in type A, the only case the paper uses. Suppose Ext¹_G(L(ω_κ),L(ω)) ≠ 0 with ω ∈ X⁰(T). Then λ := ω_κ−ω is dominant, nonzero and in W_p·0 (mod X⁰). Write λ+η ≡ w(η)+pν with ν a nonzero element of the root lattice. Dominance of λ+η and p > h−1 force ν to be weakly decreasing, so ν1−νn ⩾ 2 and ⟨λ,α0^∨⟩ ⩾ 2p−2(h−1) ⩾ 2(h−1). This contradicts ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ < 2(h−1). So a false intermediate claim sits in the proof of a true lemma. The lemma is only applied under large genericity, where p is large. Versions: the same sentence is in v3 and v4 (v4 p. 62); v2 has the analogous '< 2(n−1) ⩽ p−2'.

review.reason: Confirmed as an error in the proof. Lemma 4.2.4 is stated under `Assume that $p\geq2(h-1)$', and the step asserts `As $\langle\omega_\kappa,\alpha^\vee\rangle<2(h-1)\leq p-2$ … it follows that $\omega_\kappa$ lies in the lower $p$-restricted alcove'. The chain $2(h-1)\leq p-2$ is two more than the hypothesis supplies, and it fails exactly at $p\in\{2h-2,2h-1\}$; the finding's $h=3$, $p=5$, $\omega_\kappa=(3,0,0)$ is on the upper wall, since $\langle\omega_\kappa+\rho,\alpha_0^\vee\rangle=5=p$. Being in the restricted region is in any case weaker than being in the lowest alcove, which is what the Ext-vanishing conclusion uses.

review.reason: Confirmed verbatim: `Since $\Inj(F(\mu))$ is rigid (it is isomorphic to $\Proj(F(\mu))$), this is the unique increasing Loewy series.' sourceIssues.correction: Replace 'lie in different alcoves sharing a face' by the actual Ext¹ pattern (as in [And87, §4.1] and Table 6). In Table 5 labels the nonzero pairs among {A,…,G} are A–B, A–E, A–F, B–C, B–D, C–E, C–F, D–E, D–F, E–G, F–G. Alternatively, state only what is used: Ext¹ ≠ 0 forces λ_i = θ_i for i ≠ i₀, and dim Ext¹ ≤ 1.
sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample from the paper's own results. Take f = 1 and λ 6-deep in A, and let θ := w̃_E·λ = (12)t_{α₂}·λ, which lies in E and is 6-deep. By Lemma 4.2.6's proof and Table 5 (row E), L(θ) is a summand of gr₁Q₁(λ). By (4.8) (ξ = 0), Q₁(λ) is injective among p-bounded modules, so Ext¹_G(L(θ), L(λ)) ≅ Hom_G(L(θ), gr₁Q₁(λ)) ≠ 0. But A ⊂ (0,p)³ and E ⊂ (0,p)×(p,2p)×(2p,3p) (pairings with α₁^∨, α₂^∨, α₀^∨) share no face, not even a vertex. Table 6 likewise draws arrows A–E, A–F, C–F and D–E between non-adjacent alcoves. In the paper's defence, the proof of Proposition 4.2.12 (p. 94) uses the correct pattern ('λ_{i₀} ∈ D ⇒ θ_{i₀} ∈ E or F; λ_{i₀} ∈ F ⇒ θ_{i₀} ∈ C, D or G', matching Table 6), and the other uses (uniqueness of M, existence of i₀) only need dim ≤ 1 and the Künneth reduction, so the downstream results are unaffected. Independent check: Statement checked on p. 91. Encode an alcove by (⌊⟨x+η,α1^∨⟩/p⌋, ⌊⟨x+η,α2^∨⟩/p⌋, ⌊⟨x+η,α0^∨⟩/p⌋). Table 5 and Table 6 then give: A = (0,0,0), B = (0,0,1), {C,D} = {(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}, {E,F} = {(1,0,2),(0,1,2)}, G = (1,1,2). With Table 6's own weights, C = (1,0,1), D = (0,1,1), E = (1,0,2), F = (0,1,2); Table 5's permutation convention swaps the letters but not the geometry. Two of these alcoves share a face iff their triples differ in exactly one entry by 1. So A shares a face only with B, and A–E, A–F, C–F and D–E are non-adjacent pairs. The closures of A and E are disjoint (α0-pairings in (0,p) and (2p,3p)). The paper itself gives nonzero Ext¹ for these pairs. On p. 93, 'gr₁Q₁(λ⁰_{i₀}) is the direct sum of three irreducible modules in alcoves … B, E, and F if λ⁰_{i₀} is in alcove A'. Table 6 (second diagram) puts A = L(μ) in the socle of V(μ^op+pη′) ⊂ Q₁(μ) with E and F in the next layer, and the first diagram has edges A–E, A–F, C–F and D–E. Since Q₁(λ) has simple socle L(λ), each L(θ) ⊂ gr₁Q₁(λ) gives a nonsplit extension, so Ext¹_G(L(θ),L(λ)) ≠ 0. This holds for 6-deep λ ∈ A and θ = w̃_E·λ ∈ E, so the 'only if' direction is false. Every face-sharing pair in {A,…,G} is an edge of Table 6, so the 'if' direction and dim ⩽ 1 are not contradicted. The proof of Proposition 4.2.12 (p. 94) cites 4.2.9 for 'λ_{i₀} in D (resp. F) ⇒ θ_{i₀} in E or F (resp. C, D, or G)'. That is the Table 6 pattern, not face-sharing (D shares a face with only one of E, F, and F none with C), so the downstream arguments are unaffected. Versions: new in v4 (p. 67) with the same wording; v3 instead asserted existence of i₀ and uniqueness of M, citing [Hum06, §12.6].

sourceIssues.reason: τ_S has lowest-alcove parameter μ + s(w̃^*)^{−1}(0) − η and τ'_S has μ + s(w̃')^{−1}(0) − η; their difference s((w̃')^{−1}(0) − (w̃^*)^{−1}(0)) pairs with coroots by up to 2 in the cases actually used. Computed: for w̃^* = α and the triple (ε1−ε2, 0, ε2−ε1), (5.5) forces w̃' = γ^+α; in the n = 0 base case with w̃^* = id and σ_i = (ε1,1), the only admissible w̃' are γ^+β, βγ^+, βγ^+β; in both situations the translation parts differ by (1,2,0) or (1,−1,0), of spread 2. So τ'_S may be only (13−2)-generic. Lemma 5.1.3 uses Proposition 4.3.7 and Theorem 4.1.9 for σ(τ'_S), both stated for 13-generic representations, and the proof of Theorem 4.1.9 through Prop. 4.3.7 needs 13 to produce an auxiliary 10-generic ρ̄ (13 − 3). Defence: the constant 13 may have slack, and ρ̄_S is already 10-generic here; but the paper does not address the genericity of τ'_S at all. Independent check: Quotations checked on pp. 113–114. The auxiliary type τ′_S = τ(s(w′)^{−1}, μ+s(w̃′)^{−1}(0)) has lowest alcove parameter shifted from that of τ_S by δ = s((w̃′)^{−1}(0)−(w̃*)^{−1}(0)). This δ lies in the root lattice mod X⁰, because Adm(η) ⊂ t_ηW_a and η ≡ η′ = α0 mod X⁰. A nonzero element of the A2 root lattice pairs with some coroot to absolute value at least 2. So whenever the parameter moves, a 13-generic τ_S only guarantees that τ′_S is 11-generic (take μ exactly 13-deep on the relevant wall). The parameter does move in cases the proof needs. Example: in the n = 0 case of Lemma 5.1.4 with w̃*_i = id and σ_i = (ε1,1), a finite w′ of length ⩾ 2 cannot work, because (ε1,1) ∈ w′^{−1}(Σ0) forces w′(ε1) ∈ {0,ε1,ε2} ∩ Wε1 = {ε1}, hence w′ ∈ {1,β}. So w̃′ has a nonzero translation part mod X⁰. The readers' enumeration (checked by rerunning it and against the definitions on pp. 18–20, including that W̃ acts only on the first factor of Λ_W×A) gives γβ, βγ, βγβ with shift of spread 2, and for (5.5) with w̃* = α it forces γα with spread 2. Lemma 5.1.3 for τ′_S uses Proposition 4.3.7 and Theorem 4.1.9 for σ(τ′_S). Both are stated for 13-generic R, and their proofs need 13 − 3 = 10-generic auxiliary ρ̄ to exist (p. 101, via Proposition 3.4.5). The paper never addresses the genericity of τ′_S. Salvaging part of this with the given 10-generic ρ̄_S is possible for Proposition 4.3.7 but not obviously for Theorem 4.1.9.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap in the genericity bookkeeping. The two auxiliary types are $\tau_\cS=\tau(s(w^*)^{-1},\mu+s(\tld w^*)^{-1}(0))$ and $\tau'_\cS=\tau(s(w')^{-1},\mu+s(\tld w')^{-1}(0))$, whose lowest-alcove parameters differ by $s((\tld w')^{-1}(0)-(\tld w^*)^{-1}(0))$; the elements substituted are of length up to two more, so the depth can drop, and the results invoked for $\tau'_\cS$ (Theorem 4.1.9, Proposition 4.3.7) carry a 13-generic hypothesis that is not re-checked. Raising the hypothesis of Theorem 5.1.1, as the correction proposes, is the clean fix. I verified the two type formulas and the 13-generic hypothesis of Proposition 4.3.7 directly; the exact loss per case rests on the finding's computation.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1, proofs of Lemma 5.1.4 (n = 0) and Lemma 5.1.5, published pp. 113–114; arXiv v4 pp. 85–86
sourceIssues.printed: there is still a surjection σ̄(τ_S)^σ ↠ V by (5.5) and Theorem 4.1.9.
sourceIssues.correction: V is defined as a quotient of σ̄(τ_S)^σ. To apply Lemma 5.1.3 (resp. the induction) for another type τ'_S one needs V to be isomorphic, as a G-module, to a quotient of σ̄(τ'_S)^σ. Theorem 4.1.9 and Proposition 4.1.1 only give that the quotient of σ̄(τ'_S)^σ with Jordan–Hölder set JH(V) exists and has the same pointing graph. An argument that the two multiplicity-free modules (same cosocle, constituents and extension graph, coming from lattices in different Deligne–Lusztig representations) are isomorphic is missing.
sourceIssues.reason: Two multiplicity-free modules with the same constituents and the same Γ need not be isomorphic in general (e.g. a 'diamond' σ over κ1 ⊕ κ2 over κ carries a gluing parameter when the relevant Yoneda products in Ext^2 vanish). So 'by Theorem 4.1.9' does not suffice as stated. Defence: the claim is very plausibly true for these specific modules, for instance via multiplicity-one statements in projective envelopes as in Lemma 4.2.14, or via the Weyl-module embedding of §4.2.4. EGS15 handles the analogous GL2 step at the level of patched modules (proof of their Lemma 10.1.12). Independent check: Checked on pp. 111–114. Lemma 5.1.3 (applied to τ′_S in the n = 0 case of Lemma 5.1.4) and the induction after the type change in Lemma 5.1.5 both need V itself to be a quotient of σ̄(τ′_S)^σ. V is given as a quotient of σ̄(τ_S)^σ. Theorem 4.1.9 with Propositions 4.1.1–4.1.2 yields only a quotient V″ of σ̄(τ′_S)^σ with JH(V″) = JH(V) and the same graph Γ. I found nothing in the paper showing that a multiplicity-free module with cosocle σ is determined by JH and Γ; a search for such a uniqueness statement came up empty. In general it is not: in a 'diamond' σ over κ1⊕κ2 over κ with vanishing Yoneda products in Ext², the two extension classes glue with a free parameter. Lemma 3.6.2 does not rescue the argument either. It makes M∞(V) ≅ R∞/I(V) depend only on JH(V) once M∞(V) is cyclic, but cyclicity is the point at issue, and two MCM modules with the same reduced support need not both be cyclic. For f = 1 the small V's in the n = 0 case are determined (Ext¹ is one-dimensional), so the problem arises from f ⩾ 2 or larger V. EGS15 (Lemma 10.1.12) identify the lattice explicitly for the analogous GL2 step, but only in length 2. The claim is very plausible, but the justification 'by (5.5) and Theorem 4.1.9' is incomplete.

The printed step is `there is still a surjection $\ovl\sigma(\tau_\cS)^\sigma\twoheadrightarrow V$ by (5.5) and Theorem 4.1.9', and what the induction then needs is that $V$ is a quotient of $\ovl\sigma(\tau'_\cS)^\sigma$ for the new type. The standing assumption (p. 111: 'we assume that the weight σ satisfies the conditions of Theorem 5.1.1', and p. 112) is that V is a quotient of σ̄(τ_S)^σ with σ satisfying (5.1), i.e. a_i = 1 whenever ℓ(w̃_i^*) ⩽ 1 (Proposition 2.1.3(1): Tr_μ(ω,a) lies in alcove π^{−1}(a)). The paper puts (w̃*_{i′})^{−1}(ν4,1) in Σ_{V²,i′} as a socle constituent, and Σ_{V²,i′} has exactly 2 elements. In the extension graph, adjacent vertices have different a. So the other i′-constituent, which must point to it for V² to have simple cosocle, has a = 0. But ℓ(w̃*_{i′}) ⩽ 1 (this is forced by #(Σ_{V,i′}∩r(Σ0)) = 5; ℓ ⩾ 2 rows of Table 3 have at most 4 predicted weights). So cosoc(V²) violates (5.1). If V² had non-simple cosocle it would not be a quotient of any σ̄(τ_S)^{σ″}, which is even further from the hypothesis. Either way, 'by the inductive hypothesis' does not literally apply. The argument of Lemma 5.1.4 plausibly extends, since only the shape of Σ_{V²,i′} matters, but this is not stated. A minor gap.

review.reason: Confirmed. The statement as printed is false for Cohen–Macaulay sheaves that are not of full support: for $\cM=\cO_C$ with $C$ a component of the special fibre meeting another component along a divisor of $C$ inside $Z$, $\cM$ is Cohen–Macaulay but has depth one at the generic point of that intersection, so $H^1_Z(\cM)\neq0$ and $j_*j^*\cM\supsetneq\cM$. The codimension-two argument needs depth at least two along $Z$, which is what maximal Cohen–Macaulayness over the Cohen–Macaulay $X_\infty(\tau_\cS)$ supplies, and the sheaves it is applied to, $M_\infty(\sigma(\tau_\cS)^\circ)$, are of that kind. Note that E89 records the same sentence and the same correction; see the verdict there.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. The printed step is `That $R^{\mathrm{univ}}_\tau$ is finite over $\cO_E$ implies that there is a conjugate self-dual lift $r:G_F\ra\GL_3(\ovl\Q_p)$ of $\rbar$ …'. Finiteness over $\cO_E$ is compatible with $R^{\mathrm{univ}}_\tau=0$, which would produce no lift at all; what is needed in addition is that the ring is nonzero of dimension at least one, which the usual presentation of the global deformation ring over the local lifting rings supplies. The recorded correction names exactly that missing input.
